relearning.title: Read: comparing ionic and covalent compounds
relearning.description: A short reading with the lunch-money and shared-pizza analogy, worked examples and quick checks.

body.text:
**I can compare ionic and covalent compounds.**

**Think of lunch money vs. a shared pizza.** If a friend hands you a dollar, the dollar moves from them to you: one gives and one takes. That is an **ionic** bond. If you and a friend split a pizza, nobody gives it away; you both eat from it. That is a **covalent** bond.

**What they are made of.** Metal + nonmetal makes an **ionic** compound. Two or more nonmetals make a **covalent** compound. Metals sit **left of the staircase** on the periodic table. Transition metals like iron and copper are metals too. Hydrogen is a nonmetal, even though it sits on the left.

**What the electrons do.** Ionic: the metal **transfers** electrons to the nonmetal. That makes positive and negative **ions** that attract. Covalent: the atoms **share** electrons. That makes **molecules**.

**One special case.** A compound with a **polyatomic ion** is **ionic**. That includes **ammonium, NH₄⁺**, even though ammonium compounds have no metal.

**Worked example:** CaBr₂ and PBr₃. Calcium is a metal, so CaBr₂ is ionic: calcium transfers electrons to bromine. Phosphorus is a nonmetal, so PBr₃ is covalent: the atoms share electrons.

checks.explanation: Potassium is a metal (left of the staircase) and chlorine is a nonmetal, so KCl is ionic. CH₄ and SO₂ are only nonmetals, so they are covalent. Calling CH₄ ionic because hydrogen sits on the left is the common mistake: hydrogen is a nonmetal.

checks.prompt: In an ionic bond, electrons are transferred. In a covalent bond, electrons are ___. Type one word.
checks.explanation: Covalent bonds share electrons, like splitting a pizza. Ionic bonds transfer them, like handing over a dollar. Mixing the two up is the common mistake.

sections.title: Properties and names

body.text:
**Properties are your evidence.** Ionic compounds have **high melting points** (generally above 300 °C), form hard **crystals** and **conduct electricity when dissolved in water**, because they break into free-moving ions. Covalent compounds have **low melting points**, can be solid, liquid or gas, and **do not conduct** when dissolved, because they stay as whole molecules. Color, mass and where a bottle was stored are **irrelevant evidence**.

**They are named differently too.** Ionic: the metal, then the nonmetal with -ide, with **no prefixes**, and a **Roman numeral** when the metal has more than one charge. Covalent: **prefixes** count the atoms.

**Worked example 2:** CaCl₂ and SCl₂ both have two chlorines. CaCl₂ is ionic, so it is **calcium chloride**. SCl₂ is covalent, so it is **sulfur dichloride**.

**Worked example 3:** An unknown melts at 80 °C and its solution does not light the bulb. 80 °C is far below 300 °C, which points to covalent. No conductivity means no free ions, which also points to covalent. Answer: **covalent**.

**Worked example 4:** (NH₄)₃PO₄ (ammonium is NH₄⁺, phosphate is PO₄³⁻). Every atom is a nonmetal, but it is made of polyatomic ions, so it is **ionic**.

**Watch out for:** calling an ammonium compound covalent just because it has no metal, calling hydrogen a metal, calling two metals (like Ca and Mg) ionic, putting prefixes on an ionic name, and using color, mass or "it dissolves" as evidence. Use melting point and conductivity instead.

checks.prompt: An unknown white solid melts at 750 °C, and its solution lights the bulb. Which conclusion is best?

options.text: Ionic: the high melting point and the conductivity both point to ionic
Covalent: it is a white solid

checks.explanation: Melting above 300 °C and conducting when dissolved both point to ionic. Color and dissolving are irrelevant evidence, and using them is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: MgO and CO each have one oxygen atom. Which names are correct?
checks.explanation: MgO is ionic, so no prefixes: magnesium oxide. CO is covalent, so the second element gets a prefix: carbon monoxide. Using one naming system for both is the common mistake.

relearning.title: Do: flip the comparison, then sort the compounds
relearning.description: Flashcards with a 3-question self-quiz, then a guess-and-flip deck of compounds and lab clues.

cards.back: Ionic: a metal and a nonmetal. Covalent: two or more nonmetals.
Ionic: transferred, like handing a friend a dollar. Covalent: shared, like splitting a pizza.
Ionic: positive and negative ions. Covalent: molecules.
Ionic: high (generally above 300 °C), hard crystals. Covalent: low; can be a solid, liquid or gas.
Ionic: conducts electricity, because the ions move freely. Covalent: does not conduct.
Ionic: no prefixes; a Roman numeral for a metal with more than one charge. Covalent: prefixes count the atoms.
A compound with a polyatomic ion, like ammonium (NH₄⁺), is ionic, even with no metal.

checks.explanation: Sodium is a metal (left of the staircase) and fluorine is a nonmetal, so NaF is ionic. CO₂ and PCl₃ have only nonmetals, so they are covalent. Skipping the metal check is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Which kind of compound conducts electricity when it is dissolved in water?
checks.explanation: Dissolved ionic compounds break into free-moving ions that carry the current. Covalent compounds stay as whole molecules, so they don't conduct.

checks.prompt: NH₄NO₃ has no metal (ammonium is NH₄⁺ and nitrate is NO₃⁻). How should it be classified?

options.text: Covalent, because every atom is a nonmetal
Ionic, because it is made of polyatomic ions
Covalent, because it has three elements

checks.explanation: A compound with a polyatomic ion is ionic, and NH₄NO₃ is made of two of them. Using only the nonmetal rule is the common mistake.

sections.title: Guess, then flip: sort the compounds

cards.back: Ionic. Potassium is a metal and iodine is a nonmetal. KI: potassium iodide.
Covalent. Both are nonmetals, so the atoms share electrons. SO₂ is sulfur dioxide.
Ionic. Copper is a transition metal, and transition metals are still metals. CuCl₂ is copper(II) chloride.
Covalent. Hydrogen is a nonmetal, even though it sits on the left. H₂O is covalent.
Ionic. It is made of polyatomic ions, so (NH₄)₂SO₄ is ionic even with no metal.

cards.front: Unknown A: melts at 801 °C, and its solution lights the bulb
cards.back: Ionic. A melting point above 300 °C and conducting when dissolved both point to ionic.

cards.front: Unknown B: melts at 45 °C, and its solution does not light the bulb
cards.back: Covalent. A low melting point and no free ions both point to covalent.

checks.prompt: Which list has ONLY covalent compounds?
checks.explanation: CO₂, N₂O and CCl₄ are only nonmetals with no polyatomic ion, so all three are covalent. CaO has calcium, a metal, and NaCl, KBr and CuO each start with a metal. Missing one hidden metal in a list is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Ionic compounds conduct electricity when dissolved because they break into free-moving ___. Type one word.
checks.explanation: Dissolved ionic compounds break into free-moving ions that carry the current. Covalent compounds stay as whole molecules, so they don't conduct. Saying "electrons" is the common mistake.

sections.title: Ionic or covalent? Deciding from the elements

checks.explanation: Nitrogen and oxygen are both nonmetals, so NO₂ is covalent: the atoms share electrons. LiF and FeCl₃ have a metal (iron is a transition metal, still a metal), and NH₄Br has the polyatomic ion ammonium, so all three are ionic.

checks.prompt: HCl is made of hydrogen and chlorine. Is it ionic or covalent? Type one word.
checks.explanation: Hydrogen is a nonmetal even though it sits on the left of the periodic table, so HCl is two nonmetals: covalent. Calling hydrogen a metal is the common mistake.
